hints: What goes wrong if you start writing zeros into grid the moment you see a 0? Think about how a freshly written zero could fool the rest of your scan.

Split the work into two passes. Pass 1 only records which rows and which columns contain an original zero (two boolean arrays). Pass 2 sets a cell to 0 if its row or its column is marked. The function changes grid in place and returns nothing.

1. Make zeroRow[rows] and zeroCol[cols], all false.
  2. For every cell equal to 0, mark its row and its column.
  3. For every cell, if zeroRow[i] or zeroCol[j], set it to 0.
  4. Return nothing; grid holds the result.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Copy the grid; for each original zero (found in the copy), write zeros across its row and column in grid.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Mark zero rows and zero columns in two boolean arrays, then fill zeros in a second pass.

explain: In the sample the only zero is at row 1, column 1, so zeroRow[1] and zeroCol[1] are marked. In pass 2, every cell in row 1 and every cell in column 1 becomes 0, so grid ends as [[1, 0, 1], [0, 0, 0], [1, 0, 1]]. Keeping the markers separate from the grid guarantees only original zeros spread. Zeroing during the scan would wrongly turn the whole grid to zeros.
recognize: "For every original zero, clear its row and column" → record first, modify later (two-pass with row/column markers).
